about: THE CARDS OF ENGLAND, SOUTH AND EAST (region england_south_east: Lundenwic, Hamwic, Gipeswic, Sarre, Fordwic, Dofras, Dommoc). Written 7 Oct 2026 by the region's weaver from the ports' places files (Data/places/<port>.json), the dossiers (Design/content/dossiers) and the spine (Design/content/spine.json). A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. Each card names its port with port.id in its 'when' and is listed in its site's 'do' in the places file; where a card carries a story's beat the beat names it. The words are in Data/writing/england_south_east.json under england_south_east.<port>.<card>.<slot>, with a picture line for each card as art.<card id>. The spine's thread flags are set only for the step they name (bs_ban_heard, sv_first_dirham, sv_scale, bk_knows_worth, bk_parchment, bk_carried, hy_fed_poor, hy_sold_dear, df_warned); the places files' own flags are kept as they are written there (dofras_*, dommoc_*, fordwic_riddle_*); this file's flags begin ese_. Grand rewards are unlock_ flags (Design/content/CHAINS.md), given only where a places file's unlock says how. Lines that run through several ports: the wolf pennies (Gipeswic, Dommoc, Dofras), the cable (Dommoc, Gipeswic), the Sheldrake (Sarre, Lundenwic), the wool man's tally (Lundenwic, Hamwic), the priest's letter (Lundenwic, Fordwic), the little scale (Sarre, Fordwic), the potter's crate (Gipeswic, Dommoc), the cousins' message (Dofras, Lundenwic), the moneyer's son (Gipeswic, Dommoc, 991), the widow's silver (Hamwic, 838 and after). Every source is in the card's 'note'; (?) marks what was not checked.

cards.note: Lundenwic, the hard: a deal in the years of the ban. A Frankish wine ship is not let land and her master sells over the side, unwitnessed (places/lundenwic.json, Tatberht's rumour: 'He sold his wine to a Frisian over the side. Everybody saw; nobody witnessed'). The ban of about 789 to 796: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12; no reeve is recorded turning Franks away (dossier lundenwic 8) (?). Witnessed buying in the wic: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16. Wine 60 d the cask (goods_793.json). Being seen sets ese_unwitnessed, which the lawsuit card reads; sending him west sets ese_frank_sent_west, which the Hamwic ale-house reads. The master is invented.

cards.note: Lundenwic, the king's hall: a riddle given, and the spine's hook for riddle_road here ('At Lundenwic the king's toll-reeve gives the ice riddle for the same at London'). The reeve is lundenwic.wighelm (cast.wighelm; invented, the office real). The riddle is Exeter Book 68-69, ice (riddles_793.json riddle_exeter_68_69_ice, given by 'the king's toll-reeve' with the reward rw_toll_lundenwic); as he says it, it is our own plain rendering (the text exeter_68_69_ice in texts_793.json; Tupper 1910). Answered, it sets unlock_charter_lundenwic for four years ('for some years'). Stories lundenwic.water_made_bone beat 2 and fordwic.sword_and_sheath beat 4. The fourth choice closes harbour.forty_crates.gipeswic (the potter's toll on forty crates: the ties gipeswic.tilbeorht and lundenwic.wighelm).

cards.note: Lundenwic, the king's hall: a lawsuit and an oath. By the law of the Kentish kings a man of Kent who buys in the wic of London has two or three honest men or the king's wic-reeve as witness; if the goods are claimed from him he vouches the seller to warranty 'at the king's hall in the wic', and failing that swears 'at the altar' that he bought openly (Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16; Thatcher 1907; dossier lundenwic 1, 6; wording to check (?)). Here the merchant is the seller vouched. The reeve is lundenwic.wighelm to 810 and his successors after; the priest lundenwic.eanwulf to 812, then a priest of Saint Paul's; the buyer is invented. Quernstones 12 d the pair (goods_793.json).

cards.note: Lundenwic, the moneyers' benches: Ibba (lundenwic.moneyer), a moneyer named on Offa's pennies (Naismith, British Numismatic Journal 80, 2010; dossier lundenwic 3). The spine's easter egg for silver_road here: 'a moneyer shows a gold piece with marks nobody can read, copied from a coin a pilgrim brought'. The piece is Offa's gold dinar (British Museum), copied from a dinar of the caliph al-Mansur dated AH 157, 773-774, with OFFA REX set into it; that Ibba cut it is the game's (?). A merchant who has held a dirham (the thread's flag sv_first_dirham, set elsewhere) can tell him whose writing it is. The heavy penny of 792/3: chronicle_793.json 793-offa-heavy-penny. With the old scale from Thanet (ese_old_scale: harbour.little_scale.sarre) he teaches the weights and sets the thread's flag sv_scale (story sarre.little_scale beat 4).

Six cloaks at the maker's price, 15 d each (wool_cloth 18 d in goods_793.json): 45 d now, 45 d when they come off the loom (harbour.cloaks_off_the_loom.lundenwic, a fortnight on). cards.note: Lundenwic inside the walls, Aethelred's hithe, 896-897: a deal out of the Chronicle. The reeve is lundenwic.reeve (Wynsige, invented): 'There is good oak cheap on the shore this month.' Oak 30 d the load (goods_793.json); a land without trees pays more.

cards.note: Hamwic, the wic-hythe: the pilot Eadhun (hamwic.eadhun; invented). The double high water, the thirteen kilometres of even soundings and the soft mud 'safe for any body to rest on': a seventeenth-century account quoted by Morton 1992 (dossier hamwic 1). Beaduheard the reeve killed at Portland about 789 by three shiploads he took for traders: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787. Three hirings make him friendly, and then he teaches the water: unlock_pilot_solent, as the places file's unlock hamwic.unlock.solent_water says. His other ending to the long song: the ties dofras.pilot and hamwic.eadhun (story dofras.dead_light).

cards.note: Hamwic, the wic-hythe: a passenger to carry. About 721 Willibald, his father and his brother took ship near 'the mart called Hamwic', paid their fares to the master and pitched their tents by the Seine at Rouen (Huneberc, Hodoeporicon; Morton 1992; not quoted, Talbot 1954 is not free). True pilgrims pass free of toll in Francia (Pippin's capitulary of about 754-755; Charles to Offa, 796). The priest is hamwic.ceolhelm, who sends a riddle a year to the singing canon at Rouen (rotomagus.hildhard, to 811); the pilgrim is invented.

cards.note: Hamwic, the king's yard, on a feast day (Feasts.On): King Beorhtric's reeve (hamwic.reeve, Herewald; invented, the dossier assumes a reeve and names none) keeps open board for the masters who feed his beach. Beorhtric married Offa's daughter Eadburh in 789 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787); how far the ban on Frankish ships reached is not recorded, and the game lets this wic stay half open (the spine, black_stones, hook for Hamwic) (?). The bronze spoon with two prongs at its other end is a find from the supposed king's enclosure (site SOU 47; Morton 1992). A cask on his table and his own witness for your sales: the unlock hamwic.unlock.reeves_witness. Story hamwic.back_door beat 6.

cards.note: Hamwic, Beorngyth's ale-house: a rumour that is not true. A Frankish master says his king has lifted the order against English merchants; he has not, and will not until the letter of 796 (Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12; Charles to Offa, 796). 'A Frank sat on it all last week telling me what his king would do. Then his king did not' (places/hamwic.json, Beorngyth). The truth comes a moon later (harbour.franks_word_wind.hamwic, scheduled). Cloth bought tonight costs 20 d the bolt (wool_cloth 18 d in goods_793.json), and cannot lawfully be landed in Francia while the ban holds. If the Frank was sent here from the Strand (ese_frank_sent_west: harbour.wine_over_the_side.lundenwic) he says so. The Frank is invented.

cards.note: Gipeswic, the Cornhill, 880 to 912: a Danish town in a Danish land. Toki (gipeswic.toki; invented) weighs silver. Guthrum's army 'settled, and divided the land' in 880 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle); the pennies in Saint Edmund's name are struck from about 890-895 by the people who killed him; Sunday marketing forfeits the goods (Laws of Edward and Guthrum 7; Thorpe 1840); the town's bank and ditch are raised about 900-917 (dossier gipeswic 2, 5). A morning at his scale teaches the nick and the bend and sets the thread's flag sv_scale. If the last bishop's seal was sold to the army (dommoc_seal_sold) he has seen it since (story dommoc.last_seal, ending to_the_scales). Story gipeswic.horsed beat 5.

cards.note: Gipeswic, the potters' corner: Tilbeorht (gipeswic.tilbeorht; invented). cards.note: Sarre, the king's toll place: the card that opens on arrival. In 763 or 764 King Eadberht of Kent gave the minster in Thanet the toll on two ships that was his by right 'in the place called ad Serrae', and freed a third at Fordwic and Seorre: toll here went by the ship (Sawyer 29; dossier sarre 1, 4). Nothing says the toll was still taken in 793, or that it had stopped: the game takes it (dossier 8) (?). The toll man is sarre.tollman (Dunwalh; invented), whose wife is the wic-reeve's sister (cast.wighelm). By the ship: 2 d and no toll on sales this call. The abbess's freedom is the flag unlock_charter_sarre (sarre.abbess_freedom); a fast friend is passed at the slack (sarre.tollmans_slack). Stories sarre.third_ship beat 2, lundenwic.reeves_question (the beat at the toll place).

cards.note: Sarre, Tidburh's ale-house (sarre.alewife; invented): a riddle given, and the start of her story. She keeps an oyster bed and gives Exeter Book riddle 77, the oyster (riddles_793.json riddle_exeter_77_oyster, 'an oyster-gatherer of the Wantsum', reward a night's lodging); as she says it, it is our own rendering (the text exeter_77_oyster; Tupper 1910). The oysters of Richborough were famous in Roman times; Roman pits full of oyster shell were dug at Sarre (Brent 1863). Her husband's ship the Sheldrake went out by the North-mouth nine summers ago (places/sarre.json): asking after her sets ese_sheldrake_asked, answered on the breaking beach at Lundenwic (harbour.breaking_beach.lundenwic) and told in harbour.duck_on_the_shelf.sarre. cards.note: Sarre, the abbess's ship-house: a commission. The nun is sarre.cwenburh (invented; the abbess of 793 is not known). The minster in Thanet had ships free of toll at Sarre, Fordwic and London (Sawyer 29, 86, 91, 143); the clause she quotes on a ship 'worn out with great age' is Sawyer 29 in the dossier's rendering. A church wants wine and wax (dossier 4); while the two kings' ports are shut no Frankish cask may land at Lundenwic (the spine, black_stones). Saint Mildrith's day is 13 July, a fortnight after Saint Peter's. Rhenish wine 60 d the cask, wax 40 d the cake (goods_793.json); the minster pays over. Story sarre.third_ship, the beat added at the ship-house.

cards.note: Sarre, the ploughland under the down: a riddle given, and the thread silver_road. The ploughman is sarre.bynna (invented), 'the ploughman of Thanet' who gives Exeter Book riddle 21, the plough (riddles_793.json riddle_exeter_21_plough); his own short riddle is the places file's, on that riddle's lines, not a quotation. What his plough turns up is of the kind Brent dug from grave 26 on Sarre down: a bronze balance with nineteen weights, some of them Roman coins ground down, beside a man with shield and spear (Archaeologia Cantiana 6, 1866). Bought (ese_old_scale), the weights are taught by a moneyer at Canterbury or Lundenwic (harbour.eobas_bench.fordwic, harbour.moneyers_pan.lundenwic), which sets the thread's flag sv_scale. Story sarre.little_scale beat 1, endings to_sea and reburied.

cards.note: Sarre, the old graves on the down: a rumour that is true. From the down both mouths of the strait and the sea off the Foreland can be seen ('commanding the country for miles around': Brent 1863). While King Offa's shore is shut to Frankish hulls (about 789 to 796; the spine, black_stones), Frankish wine ships turned off the Strand come back down the strait loaded, and wine is dear at Lundenwic for a month: a true word, worth carrying. No reeve is recorded turning Franks away (dossier lundenwic 8) (?). The ploughman is sarre.bynna, who 'can see them and the toll man cannot'.

In the goods table the skins are cattle_hides, 15 d the bundle of five (?); the church pays 20. cards.note: Fordwic in King Edward's day, 1042 to 1066: a lawsuit. Bruman the port-reeve (fordwic.bruman, historical): Domesday Book's reeve who, in the time of King Edward, took the customs of foreign merchants on the two churches' land in Canterbury, and later admitted on oath that he had taken them unjustly (dossier fordwic 3). The king gave his two thirds of the borough to Saint Augustine's (Sawyer 1092); the burgesses of Dofras went quit of toll through all England (Domesday, Dover). The suit before the shire and the sums are invented. The unlock fordwic.unlock.brumans_oath. Story dofras.own_doors (the beat at the toll place).

cards.note: Dofras, the shingle, 794 to 797, for a merchant who carries Lul's purse of twelve wolf pennies (ese_wolf_purse: harbour.wolf_pennies.gipeswic). King Aethelberht of the East Angles was beheaded by Offa's order in 794 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 792 for 794); his penny shows a she-wolf and twins. The priest was a boy on the bench at Dommoc under Abbot Lull (dommoc.lull); he is invented. The endings of the story gipeswic.wolf_pennies: to_rome (ese_wolf_to_rome) and kept_one (ese_wolf_penny_kept: 'an heirloom in the chest'; no unlock id is written for it yet). cards.note: Dofras, Saint Martin's, from August 796 to the summer of 798. King Offa died on 29 July 796; Kent rose under Eadberht Praen, by later account a priest; Archbishop Aethelheard, Offa's man, left Canterbury, and Alcuin wrote telling him to go back to his flock (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 794 for 796 and 796 for 798; Alcuin, Epistolae; dossier fordwic 3). That a clerk of his household reached Dofras with a chest of the church's books is the game's own (story dofras.archbishops_chest). Alcuin held the cell of Saint Josse near Quentovic (quentovic.osmund is its guest master). The three endings: over_the_water (dofras_chest_carried, and the thread's flag bk_carried, set here at the taking since no card receives the chest at Quentovic yet), under_the_floor (dofras_chest_hidden), sold_to_kent (dofras_chest_sold, about 120 d (?)). The canon is dofras.clerk; the archbishop's clerk is invented. The red floor: the minster's floor of lime and crushed tile (Kent Archaeological Rescue Unit). The chain kentish_revolt_796 tells the rising itself. Story beat 2.

cards.note: Dommoc, the strand under the cliff, 794 to 796: the spine's hook for black_stones here. The wic-reeve's tally from the Strand is given to a merchant who has heard the ban there (the thread's flag bs_ban_heard; story dommoc.kings_penny beat 4); shown here it gives leave to land (ese_dommoc_leave; the unlock dommoc.landing_leave). cards.note: Dommoc, the bishop's house: a riddle given, and the spine's hook for riddle_road here. 'Lull abbas' signs with Bishop Tidfrith at Clofesho in 803, and Alcuin says Lull praised both East Anglian bishops to him in person (Haddan and Stubbs III, pp. 547, 551-552); that he taught at Dommoc is invented (dommoc.lull) (?). He sets Aldhelm's riddle of the writing tablets (riddles_793.json riddle_aldhelm_32_pugillares; Enigmata 32, Ehwald 1919), in our own short paraphrase, and will not hear the answer until a tablet has been handled (ese_seen_tablet: harbour.kings_grave.dommoc). Then the oyster (riddle_exeter_77_oyster) and the lighthouse (riddle_aldhelm_92_farus), whose answer stands at Dofras (harbour.dead_light.dofras). All three, and what the Orwell fowler says of the stone fort, give his letter of greeting (dommoc_lull_letter; the unlock dommoc.lulls_letter). His word for the priest at Hamwic is ese_lull_word (harbour.cask_and_cup.hamwic). From 796 he wants a passage toward Tours, where Alcuin was abbot from that year. Stories dommoc.boys_bench_riddles beats 1 and 7, dofras.dead_light beat 4.

Give for the lamp at the king's grave (3 d)
Make a vow at the grave for a safe crossing
Stand a while in the dark, and go back down to the boat

cards.note: Dommoc, the herring strand, 991 to 994: the end of an errand (scheduled by harbour.dies_and_the_boy.gipeswic; ese_dies_aboard). 'This year was Ipswich plundered; and very soon afterwards was Alderman Britnoth slain at Maldon' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 991; Ingram 1823). Hunstan (dommoc.herringman; invented) is the brother of the wife of the moneyer Leofsige (gipeswic.leofsige), whose son and spare dies come ashore here. The Battle of Maldon was made soon after the fight (texts_793.json maldon_991; the chain maldon_991 gives it by another road). A herring town of this size is Domesday's, read back two generations (?). Story gipeswic.ninety_three (the beat at the herring strand), ending carried_the_dies.
cards.when: moored and port.id = dommoc and flag.ese_dies_aboard
cards.title: The dies come ashore
cards.intention: The strand below the cliff is silver with fish and loud with gulls, and women are gutting at long trestles. A thick-set man with salt-scarred hands sees the boy on your stem and the box under his arm, and puts down his horn.

options.label: Hand over the boy and the box, and take nothing but fish
Hand them over, and stay to hear what was done at Maldon

memory.hand: brought the moneyer's son and dies to Dommoc
memory.verse: brought the boy to Dommoc and heard the Maldon verses

cards.note: Dommoc, the bishop's church, 866 to 870: the spine's thread price_of_england at its beginning. The great army wintered among the East Angles in 865-866, 'where they were soon horsed', and came back in 869; King Edmund was killed on 20 November 869 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 866, 870). Aethelwald (dommoc.aethelwald, historical) is the last bishop of Dommoc any list names; his profession to Archbishop Ceolnoth and his bronze seal, SIG EDILVVALDI EP, found near Eye about 1822, survive (Haddan and Stubbs III, pp. 659-660; Victoria History of Suffolk I). The game's years for him and his words are invented (?). The three endings of the story dommoc.last_seal: to_the_ground (dommoc_seal_buried; the unlock dommoc.name_in_the_list), to_the_scales (dommoc_seal_sold, 40 d; the deed dug_church_ground stands for the sacrilege, there being no nearer deed), stayed (dommoc_seal_refused). Sold, it is seen again at Gipeswic (harbour.pan_not_the_face.gipeswic). Story beats 2 and 4.
cards.when: moored and port.id = dommoc and year >= 866 and year <= 870 and not flag.dommoc_seal_buried and not flag.dommoc_seal_sold and not flag.dommoc_seal_refused

cards.note: Hamwic, the strand street: a deal, and the law of the witness. King Ine's law (c. 25): a trader who buys among the people up the country must do it before witnesses, and one found with stolen goods bought unwitnessed must swear himself clear or pay thirty-six shillings (Attenborough 1922; our wording). There is no market place at Hamwic: the street is the market (Morton 1992). The reeve is hamwic.reeve (Herewald; invented); his own witness, for a house that has set wine on his table, is ese_hamwic_witness (harbour.reeves_table.hamwic; the unlock hamwic.unlock.reeves_witness). A sale nobody witnessed is ese_unwitnessed, which the hall at Lundenwic remembers (harbour.sworn_at_the_hall.lundenwic). Hides 15 d the bundle (goods_793.json). The seller is invented.

cards.note: Lundenwic, the bridge, from May 1012 to 1014. Archbishop Aelfheah was killed by the army at Greenwich on 19 April 1012; 'then submitted to the king five and forty of the ships of the enemy, and promised him that they would defend this land, and he should feed and clothe them' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1012; Ingram 1823). In 1013 the town would not yield to King Swein 'because therein was King Ethelred, and Thurkil with him', and in 1014 twenty-one thousand pounds were paid to the army that lay at Greenwich (the same, 1013, 1014). That Thorkell offered all he had but his ship for the archbishop's life is Thietmar of Merseburg's telling (Chronicon VII.42-43; our wording) (?). The chief is lundenwic.thorkell; that his men kept the bridge, and his words, are invented. Wheat 6 d the sack (goods_793.json); a hungry fleet gives 8. The thread price_of_england: the spine's years of tribute.

cards.note: Lundenwic, Saint Peter's on Thorney, 1050 to 1065: a commission. King Edward's church was raised from about 1050 in the manner of the Normans and hallowed on 28 December 1065; he was buried in it at Twelfth Night (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1065; en.wikipedia Westminster Abbey). Dunstan's house of about 959 had a dozen monks. The fisherman who ferried Saint Peter to Thorney on the night before the first church was hallowed, and the salmon owed for it, are the abbey's own legend (Sulcard, about 1080) (?). That the roof was leaded with Peak lead brought by water is the game's (?). Lead 15 d the pig (goods_793.json); the king's works give 20. The cellarer is invented.

cards.note: Fordwic, the hythe at the tide's end: a deal. The river is tidal to Fordwic and no further, and what is landed here goes up to Canterbury by road (Tatton-Brown 1992; dossier fordwic 1); the later port had the sole right of lading and unlading for the city (Hasted 1800). That the two churches kept an ox cart on the hythe in 793 is the game's (?). Eadberht Praen, by later account a priest, held Kent from 796 to 798 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). Wine 60 d the cask, quernstones 12 d the pair (goods_793.json); at the cellarer's door they fetch a seventh more. The carter is invented.

Ride up on the cart tail, and see the city

cards.note: Sarre, the strand market, at harvest: a deal by the season. 'If a man of Kent buys property in London, he shall have two or three trustworthy men, or the king's wic-reeve, as witness' (Law of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16; Attenborough 1922; our wording): the two watchers by every bargain are that law read on this strand (places/sarre.json). Bede counts Thanet at six hundred households and calls it fruitful (Ecclesiastical History I.25); salt at Minster and Monkton is Domesday's. No cargo, price or market day is recorded at Sarre (dossier sarre 8). Wheat 6 d the sack, bay salt 3 d (goods_793.json); cheapest after the harvest. The farm wife is invented.

cards.note: Dofras, the trodden ground before Saint Martin's, in slaughter month: a deal by the season. The English called the eleventh month Blodmonath, the month of sacrifices, when the beasts that could not be wintered were killed (Bede, De temporum ratione 15); the town keeps its own saint's feast, Martinmas, in the same weeks (places/dofras.json, seasons). Salt is wanted and hides are cheap: bay salt 3 d the sack, salt pork 14 d the barrel, hides 15 d the bundle (goods_793.json). No market place is known at Dover in these years (dossier dofras 2, 8). The woman is invented.
